label: Part 1: The Arrival
title: North End Arrivals
body: Between 1910 and 1970 the demographic landscape of Hartford shifted dramatically. This panel explores the initial waves of the Great Migration and the community centers that took root along Main Street and Albany Avenue.
caption: Albany Avenue storefronts

label: Part 2: Building Community
title: Churches and Mutual Aid
body: New residents established churches, mutual-aid societies, and businesses that anchored a vibrant Black community in the face of housing and employment discrimination.
caption: A North End congregation

label: Part 3: Working the City
title: Industrial Opportunity
body: The promise of factory work drew families north, even as the best jobs and neighborhoods stayed closed. Labor became both a livelihood and a site of struggle.
caption: Shift change at the plant

label: Part 4: A Lasting Mark
title: Roots That Held
body: By 1940 the North End had become a cornerstone of Hartford's African American life — a legacy still visible in the city's culture and geography today.

label: Part 1: The Red Lines
title: Graded for Exclusion
body: The 1937 HOLC security map graded Hartford's neighborhoods and encoded racial exclusion into who could borrow, buy, and build.
caption: The HOLC grade map

label: Part 2: Renewal and Removal
title: What Urban Renewal Took
body: Mid-century 'renewal' cleared blocks of Black Hartford in the name of progress, displacing families and severing established neighborhoods.
caption: Demolition downtown

label: Part 3: The Fight Back
title: Organizing for Home
body: Tenants, churches, and activists organized against displacement and for fair housing across the postwar decades.

label: Part 1: The Factory Floor
title: Powering the Capital
body: Hartford's factories — from typewriters to aircraft — ran on the labor of migrants and immigrants alike.
caption: Assembly line

label: Part 2: Organizing
title: Unions and Wages
body: Workers organized for fair wages and safer conditions, with mixed access across racial lines.
